This verse opens an oath by God on several great creations, affirming that what is promised to people, the Resurrection and the recompense, will certainly come to pass. The commentators differ on who or what is meant. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, followed by Ibn Kathir, take the "mursalat" and the "'asifat" to be winds, while Abu Salih, Muqatil and al-Dahhak take them to be angels sent with God's command and prohibition. Al-Tabari holds that the oath covers everything fitting these descriptions without restriction. The word "'urfan" is understood by most as "in close succession, like the mane of a horse," while al-Zamakhshari also gives it the sense of goodness and kindness.

There is broad agreement that the "mulqiyat dhikran" are the angels who convey revelation to the prophets. For "al-fariqat farqan", some name the angels who separate truth from falsehood, others the verses of the Qur'an, and others the winds that scatter the clouds. "'Udhran aw nudhran" means a clear justification and a warning from God to His creatures; the readers differ on the vowelling, and most treat both words as verbal nouns.

Ibn Kathir considers it most likely that the first three descriptions refer to the winds, as the Qur'an itself suggests, while the later ones refer to angels, a view al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari hold in various forms. Al-Razi notes that the sequence of particles allows several meanings and leaves the matter open. The answer to the oath is that what you are promised will certainly happen, followed by the signs of the end: the stars dimmed, the sky split open, the mountains blown away.

The surah opens with God swearing by certain of His creations, and the commentators note that the named objects are left implicit, with their attributes standing in their place. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Salih and Muqatil take the mursalat (those sent) and the 'asifat (the violent ones) to be the winds, while Masruq and al-Kalbi take them to be the angels sent with God's command. On either reading, the oath confirms that what people are promised, the resurrection and the requital, will certainly come to pass.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Salih and others understand the fariqat (those who separate) as angels who divide truth from falsehood, whereas al-Hasan and Qatada take them to be the verses of the Qur'an that separate the lawful from the unlawful, and Mujahid takes them to be winds that scatter the clouds. Ibn Mas'ud and most scholars read the 'asifat as strong gusting winds, while Muslim ibn Subayh holds that they are angels who seize the soul of the unbeliever, and others see them as destructive signs such as earthquakes and eclipses.

Most commentators hold that the nashirat are winds that spread out the clouds and the rain, though Abu Salih links them to rains that revive the earth, and as-Suddi, Muqatil and Ibn 'Abbas see them as angels who unfold the records of deeds. The mulqiyat dhikran are, by broad agreement, the angels who convey revelation to the prophets, though Qutrub says they are the messengers who pass it on to their peoples. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari lean toward reading the verses as referring to both winds and angels, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that the first two terms describe winds and the rest describe angels. Readers differ over 'udhran aw nudhran, with or without shadda, but both forms are verbal nouns meaning an established excuse and a warning.

At the opening of Surat al-Mursalat, God swears by great creations, and the commentators differ on what they are. The "nashirat nashra" are, for most, winds that spread the clouds, as Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and Qatada say; for Abu Salih they are the rains that bring plants to life; for al-Suddi and al-Dahhak they are angels who unfold the records of deeds. There is agreement that the "mulqiyat dhikra" are the angels who convey revelation to the prophets, to establish proof and give warning. Ibn Mas'ud and the majority take the "'asifat 'asfa" to be violent winds, while Muslim ibn Subayh holds them to be angels. Al-Tabari concludes that the oath covers whatever the description fits, whether angels, winds or clouds.

All agree on what is sworn to: what you are promised, namely resurrection and recompense, will certainly come to pass. It will happen when the stars are extinguished, the sky is split open and the mountains are blown away, on the Day of Decision between creatures. Ibn Kathir and the majority explain that the repeated "woe" in the surah is a threat to those who denied that Day, and that some held Wayl to be a valley in Hell, a view Ibn Kathir considers unsound.

Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi report that readers differ on the vowelling of "'udhran aw nudhran": some read the consonant with a light vowel, others with a full one. Al-Tabari prefers the lighter reading while accepting the other, and Abu Ali al-Farisi holds that the fuller form may be the plural of "'adhir" and "nadhir".

This verse opens with an oath by magnificent creations of God, to affirm that what is promised to people, the Resurrection and recompense, will certainly come to pass. The commentators agree that "those who convey the reminder" are the angels. On the other descriptions they differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and Qatada, followed by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understand the first words, the "sent ones", the "violently blowing" and the "spreading", as winds: successive winds, violent winds, and winds that scatter the clouds. Others, such as Masruq, Abu Salih, Muqatil and al-Suddi, take them to be angels who carry God's commands and revelation and act in the world by His order. For "those who separate with a separation", Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak mean the angels who distinguish truth from falsehood, while Qatada and al-Hasan mean the verses of the Quran that distinguish the lawful from the unlawful. Al-Razi also considers readings in which the verses refer to the Quran or to the prophets. As for "as an excuse or a warning", most explain it as God's proof to His servants, so that they have no excuse left, while al-Zamakhshari says it may mean the excuse of the repentant or the warning to the heedless ingrates. The oath leads to its answer: what you are promised will surely happen. The following verses describe the signs of that day: the stars dimmed, the sky split open, and the mountains blown away.

At the opening of Surah al-Mursalat, God swears by several of His creations that what is promised to people, resurrection and recompense, will certainly come to pass. The phrase "fal-mulqiyati dhikran" refers, according to most commentators, to the angels who convey the revelation and the reminder to the prophets, as a proof and a warning from God to His creatures, so that they have no argument left. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and the majority say the angels convey to the prophets the revelation they carry. Qutrub holds that it is the messengers who convey what was revealed to them to their peoples, while al-Kalbi speaks of angels delivering revelation to the prophets. On the other attributes, opinions differ. Ibn Mas'ud and most commentators identify "al-mursalat", "al-'asifat" and "al-nashirat" as the winds, which spread and drive the clouds, while others take them to be angels. For "al-fariqat", Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak say it means angels who separate truth from falsehood, while Qatada and al-Hasan say it refers to the verses of the Quran that distinguish the lawful from the unlawful, and Mujahid also takes it to mean winds that scatter clouds. Al-Tabari concludes that the oath embraces all these realities, whether angels, winds or messengers. As for "'urfan", some understand it as successive, like a horse's mane, and others as goodness and kindness. The readings of "'udhran aw nudhran" vary between vocalised and unvocalised forms, but the meaning remains that of excuse and warning.

This surah opens with oaths by great creations to affirm that what is promised to people, namely resurrection and recompense, will certainly occur. The commentators differ on identifying these creations. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Abu Salih, and most scholars, take the "sent ones" and the "violent ones" to be winds that blow in succession and with great force. Masruq, Abu Hurayra and Muqatil, however, understand them as angels sent with what is good by God's command and prohibition. As for the "scatterers", some say they are winds spreading clouds, others angels who unfold the books, or rains that bring plants to life, and others the resurrection in which souls are scattered. Most say the "separators" are angels who distinguish truth from falsehood, while al-Hasan and Qatada take them to be the verses of the Quran that separate the lawful from the unlawful, and Mujahid takes them to be winds that disperse the clouds. There is agreement that the "bringers of reminder" are angels who convey revelation to the prophets. The phrase "as an excuse or as a warning" means an excuse from God to His creatures and a warning to them. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the winds serve as an excuse for those who repent and a warning to those who forget gratitude. Readers differ on the vowelling of the two words, and al-Farra' and Abu 'Ali regard the forms as dialectal variants with the same meaning. The answer to the oath is that what you are promised will surely come to pass. The following verses describe its signs: the stars going out, the sky being split open, and the mountains being blown away. Then comes the woe upon the deniers, which Ibn Mas'ud identifies as a valley in hell.

The verse opens with oaths by certain of God's creations, and its answer declares that what you are promised, the Day of Resurrection, will certainly come to pass. For the terms al-mursalat, al-'asifat, al-nashirat and al-fariqat, the commentators differ between winds and angels. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya find it most apparent that the first two refer to winds, while Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid also take them as winds, and Abu Hurayra, Masruq, Muqatil and Abu Salih take them as angels. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari connect the oaths to the Day of Resurrection. Concerning al-mulqiyat dhikran, there is near-unanimity that these are angels who convey revelation to the prophets, though some say they are messengers who pass it to their peoples. The following verses describe the signs of that event: the stars are extinguished, the sky is split, the mountains are blown away, and the messengers are gathered at an appointed time for the day of decision. Readers differ on the vocalisation of 'udhran aw nudhran and on uqqitat; al-Tabari regards the variants as dialectal forms with the same meaning, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the waw is the original letter and the hamza a substitution. Ibn Kathir reports that wayl is a valley in hell but says the report is not sound, whereas al-Qurtubi transmits it from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

This part of the surah announces that the stars will be extinguished and lose their light, that the sky will be split open and the mountains will be scattered, and that this happens when the time appointed for the messengers arrives, the Day of Decision between creatures. The commentators agree that tamas means the effacing of the stars' light. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir take it this way, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari also allow that the stars themselves may be annihilated, and al-Razi prefers the first reading because it needs no added assumption. Regarding the splitting of the sky, the common sense is that it is cleft or opened, and Ibn Kathir adds that its edges sag. For the verb nasafa, Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi speak of levelling the ground, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi describe a rapid uprooting and scattering like grain winnowed on a threshing floor. On the reading uqqitat, al-Tabari holds that all the recited variants have the same meaning and that the hamza replaces an original waw. Mujahid and Ibn Kathir explain that the messengers are gathered or summoned at their appointed time to bear witness over their peoples, while al-Razi considers it more fitting that the appointment concerns the arrival of the Resurrection. All agree that the Day of Decision is the day when God judges between people. As for the word wayl, some hold that it names a valley in hell, while others take it to mean ruin and punishment for those who deny.

This verse describes one of the signs of the Last Day: the sky is split open and cleaves apart. The commentators explain that the verb means it is split, torn or opened, so that gaps appear in it, as the Qur'an says elsewhere that the sky was opened and became gates. The verse belongs to a sequence of signs that begins with the dimming of the stars and ends with the crumbling of the mountains and the gathering of the messengers for the Day of Decision.

The commentators largely agree on the meaning of the splitting. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi understand it as a cracking or breaking apart. Ibn Kathir adds that the sky bursts open, its edges sag and its extremities crumble. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud speak of a rent and an opening. Al-Razi, citing parallel Qur'anic passages, favours a cleft, while Ibn 'Ashur offers two readings: either the cracking of the heavenly bodies if the word refers to all the heavens, or the breakdown of the atmosphere if it refers to the visible sky.

The scholars do not differ much on this point. They cite no legal ruling and no specific occasion of revelation for this verse, and the surah as a whole is considered Meccan by the majority.

This passage of Surah al-Mursalat describes the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. God affirms that what you are promised, namely resurrection and recompense, will certainly come to pass, and then lists its signs: the stars will be extinguished and lose their light, the sky will be split open and torn apart, and the mountains will be blown away. Ibn Kathir and others understand the mountains being removed from their places, while others see them crushed into dust scattered by the wind. Regarding the phrase about the messengers being gathered at an appointed time, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain it as the prophets being assembled or deferred to a fixed moment to bear witness before their peoples, and most identify that moment with the Day of Judgment, the Day of Separation. On recitation, Abu 'Amr reads the word with a waw, while the majority reads it with a hamza; al-Tabari holds that all these readings are correct and share one meaning, while Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note that the waw is the original and the hamza a substitution. The phrase asking for which day they were deferred conveys the greatness and dread of that day, and most commentators link it to the Day of Separation between creatures. The verse concludes with woe on that day to those who deny, where most take wayl to mean ruin and punishment; some report that it is a valley in Hell, a claim Ibn Kathir rejects. Several commentators explain the repetition of this verse in the surah by the variety of forms of denial.

This passage of Surat al-Mursalat affirms that what is promised to people, resurrection and recompense, will certainly come, and that it will be preceded by signs: the stars will be extinguished and lose their light, the sky will be split open, and the mountains will be uprooted and turned into scattered dust. Regarding the phrase « uqqitat », the commentators explain that the messengers will be gathered and a fixed time set for them, the time of their testimony against their nations on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari reports this meaning from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, while others such as Ibrahim, cited by al-Tabari, understand it as a promise or threat. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the appointed time has arrived. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari take the postponement to refer to the Day of Decision, when God judges between creatures. On the word « wayl », opinions differ: Ibn Abbas and others understand it as a valley in Hell, whereas Ibn Kathir considers that report unsound, and al-Zamakhshari reads it as ruin and woe. On recitation, al-Tabari holds that all the readings are correct and carry the same meaning, the hamza being a substitution for the waw. Ibn Ashur notes that the repetition of « idha » gives each sign its own emphasis.

This passage of Surat al-Mursalat affirms that the promise of resurrection will certainly come to pass, and that its signs appear when the stars are extinguished, the sky is split open and the mountains are blown away, and when the messengers are gathered at an appointed time. As for the question "for what day have they been postponed?", the commentators understand it as an exaltation and an expression of wonder at the terror of that day, which has been deferred until the Day of Judgment, the Day of Decision when God separates the creatures. The exegetes agree that the effacement of the stars means their light is extinguished or they are destroyed, that the splitting of the sky means it is cleft or torn apart, and that the destruction of the mountains means they are uprooted and scattered. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the messengers are gathered or postponed, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi report that they reach the time they were awaiting, when they appear to bear witness against their peoples. Several readings of the verb exist, and al-Tabari holds that they all carry the same meaning as well-known dialects, while al-Qurtubi explains that the hamza replaces a waw because of the heaviness of that vowel. Opinions differ on the meaning of appointing the time: Mujahid and al-Zajjaj take it as the fixing of the moment when the messengers appear as witnesses, whereas al-Razi holds that it means bringing that moment into being and prefers that it belong to the signs of the Last Day. As for the Day of Separation, the commentators agree it is the day when God divides creatures according to their deeds, toward Paradise or the Fire, and that woe is pronounced upon those who denied. Some report that wayl is a valley in Hell, transmitted by al-Nu'man ibn Bashir and Ibn Abbas, while Ibn Kathir judges that tradition unsound.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the oath opening the sura, whose subject is the certainty of what is promised, namely the resurrection and recompense. The plain meaning is that the messengers were set a fixed appointed time, and that this is the Day of Judgment, the day on which God decides between His creatures, giving the wronged their right against the wrongdoer and repaying each person according to his deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid report that the word uqqitat means that the messengers were given a term, gathered, or made to wait, while Ibn Abbas explains it as being gathered. Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj hold that the hamza replaces a waw because of the difficulty of the damma, whereas others treat the different readings as dialectal variants with a single meaning. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya note that the readings with waw and with hamza are related forms with the same sense. All agree that the day is the Day of Resurrection and that al-Fasl is the judgment between creatures. Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir say that the rhetorical question magnifies the terror of that day, and al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di add that it is the day when truth is separated from falsehood. Beyond the grammar of the verb, the commentators show little real disagreement on the meaning of the verse.

This verse, in the sura al-Mursalat, is a question of exaltation about the Day of Judgment. The commentators explain that God addresses His Prophet, telling him that he cannot grasp the reality and terror of that day unless it is made known to him. Al-Hasan al-Basri reports that the Prophet did not know its true nature until God informed him. The exegetes agree that the interrogation serves to magnify and to alarm, not to seek an answer. The Day of Separation (yawm al-fasl) is, for them, the day on which God judges between creatures: He grants the oppressed his right against the oppressor and rewards each person according to his deeds. Qatada says that on that day people are separated by their works, toward Paradise or toward the Fire, and Ibn Abbas that the Merciful will decide between the creatures.

The commentaries also agree that this magnification is followed by a threat: "Woe on that day to those who deny." All understand the deniers as those who reject the resurrection and recompense. As for the meaning of "woe" (wayl), al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as ruin and punishment, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi relate, on the authority of Nu'man ibn Bashir and Ibn Mas'ud, that it is a valley in Hell, a report Ibn Kathir judges unsound. Ibn Juzayy explains the repetition of the verse in the sura either as emphasis or as a return to what precedes it in each passage.

Al-Zamakhshari notes that "woe" is used here in indefinite, nominative form to express the permanence of perdition. Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani hold that the punishment is measured according to the seriousness of each denial.

This verse of Surah al-Mursalat declares that woe, meaning ruin and severe punishment, will fall on that Day upon those who denied what they were told, namely the resurrection and the recompense, the Day of Decision on which God will separate all creatures. The commentators place it after the description of that Day's terrors: the stars being extinguished, the sky split open, the mountains scattered, and the messengers being given an appointed time to testify against their peoples, so the threat follows directly from what precedes it. All agree that the word wayl means perdition and torment for the deniers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy explain the repetition of the verse in the surah as emphasis, while Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a graded punishment matching the gravity of each denial. On the nature of wayl, opinions differ: al-Hasan and several exegetes take it to mean the utmost evil and grief, whereas al-Nu'man ibn Bashir and Ibn Mas'ud report that it is a valley in Hell filled with various torments, a report Ibn Kathir regards as unsound. Grammatically, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi note that this indefinite noun serves as a subject because it originates as a verbal noun expressing a supplication, and it signals the lasting nature of the ruin. The common meaning remains that those who deny the Day of Decision will face ruin on that Day.

This verse recalls that God destroyed the earlier peoples who called their messengers liars, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and that He will send the later generations who follow their path the same fate. Most commentators, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, take the later people as the Meccan disbelievers, and read the destruction as punishment and annihilation in this world.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir identify the first group as Noah's people, 'Ad and Thamud, and the later group as those who follow them in disbelief, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Muqatil identify the later group as the Quraysh of Mecca. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note a variant reading, "nutbi'hum" in the jussive, which links the later peoples to Lot, Shu'ayb and Moses. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi explain that "thus do We deal with the criminals" may be a warning about this world or an announcement of punishment in the next.

Al-Razi holds that the destruction also includes blame and curse that remain after death, which he sees as a very powerful warning. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain the repetition of "woe that day to those who deny" either as emphasis or as a division of the punishment according to the gravity of each denial.

Ibn Sa'di stresses that this is God's constant way with every criminal, and that the aim is to urge the listeners to learn from what they have seen and heard.

The commentators explain that the verse recalls God's established way with peoples who rejected their messengers: He destroyed the earlier nations, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, for denying their prophets, and then made later ones follow them, those who took the same path of disbelief. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, identify the later ones as the Quraysh who denied the Prophet, and see in the verse a warning that applies to every criminal who follows the same course. Al-Tabari, however, counts the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud among the first and those of Abraham, Lot and Madyan among the later. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari report a reading with a jussive, "nutbi'hum", which links the verb to "nuhlik", so that the later ones become the people of Lot, Shu'ayb and Moses, a view Ibn al-Jawzi also records. Al-Razi considers this reading weak, because the imperfect tense points to the present and future, and he understands the earlier ones as all disbelievers before Muhammad. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the clause "thus do We deal with the criminals" clarifies the verse, and that "criminals" is a Qur'anic term for the polytheists. The overall meaning remains a warning: the fate of earlier peoples serves as an example for every criminal who persists in denial.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage warning against denial: God reminds that He destroyed the earlier nations who rejected their messengers, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and then made later ones follow the same path, and that this is His constant way with every criminal. They differ on who the 'earlier' and 'later' are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the earlier ones are the ancient peoples such as Noah's people, 'Ad and Thamud, and the later ones are those who followed their path, such as the people of Abraham, Lot and Madyan, with the warning aimed at the Quraysh of Mecca. Al-Razi considers this view weak, because the present tense covers both present and future, so he takes the later ones as future events and the earlier ones as all disbelievers before Muhammad. As for the word 'thus' (kadhalika), al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir see it either as a dreadful warning meant to teach in this world, or as an announcement of punishment in the Hereafter. On the reading, most read 'nutbi'uhum' in the nominative, while al-A'raj reads it in the jussive, coordinated with 'nuhlik'. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a rising threat rather than a mere narrative. All agree that the warning applies to anyone who commits the same sins, namely idolaters or any criminal who rebels and transgresses.

According to the commentators, this verse declares woe on that Day to those who deny the truth. It follows the mention of the earlier nations who were destroyed, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and then those who came after them, such as the people of Abraham, Lot and Madyan. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that 'the later ones' are those who followed the path of the earlier ones in disbelief, so the meaning is that We deal with the criminals in the same way, striking the deniers as their predecessors were struck. Ibn Kathir adds that this woe falls on whoever reflects on creation, which shows the greatness of its Creator, and yet persists in denial. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi allow that 'the later ones' may refer to the Quraysh, while al-Mawardi notes that the destruction may be by the sword or by general annihilation, and that 'thus do We deal' may point to a warning in this world or to punishment in the Hereafter. Al-Razi considers a destruction followed by curse and lasting punishment.

The commentators agree that the verse reinforces the threat already present in the surah. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi hold that each repetition carries a different meaning, al-Alusi distinguishes the first woe as referring to the punishment of the Hereafter and the second to that of this world, while Ibn 'Ashur sees a simple repetition meant to affirm the warning. They differ mainly over which peoples are meant and over the details of the punishment.

This verse reminds people of God's favour: He created them from a worthless fluid, the drop of semen, and placed it in a secure, firm womb until a fixed term known to Him alone, the time of birth. The commentators broadly agree on this plain meaning: the despised water is the seminal fluid, the firm place is the womb, and the appointed measure is the time of delivery. Ibn 'Abbas explains the despised water as the pure essence of water, while Mujahid and Qatada take it simply as weak water. Wahb ibn Munabbih says the womb shields the foetus from heat and cold, and al-Kalbi says it holds the fluid so that it neither returns nor spreads through the body. On the word 'faqadarna', there are two readings. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with doubling, meaning 'We decreed it', while the others read it without doubling, meaning 'We had power over it'. At-Tabari prefers the lighter reading but accepts both as valid, noting that the Arabs sometimes combine the two forms, and several scholars hold that the two mean the same thing. The verse ends with a warning to those who deny this, since the One who can create can also raise the dead, as ar-Razi observes. Ibn Sa'di adds that this measured creation shows God's continuous management of the embryo through its stages.

The commentators explain that God reminds people of their origin: He created them from a weak, despised fluid, a drop of semen, and placed it in a secure, firm lodging, the womb, until a term known to Him, the time of birth. Most agree on the meaning: the despised water is the drop of semen, the firm lodging is the womb, and the determined term is the time of delivery. Ibn 'Abbas took the sense of pure, chosen water, while Mujahid and Qatada took it to mean weak. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir stressed the womb as a place of stability. Wahb ibn Munabbih said it is protected from heat and cold, whereas al-Kalbi explained that it is guarded so the drop does not come back out or spread through the body. The readers differ on the verb 'fa-qadarna': Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a doubled letter, meaning 'we determined', while the others read it without, meaning 'we had power'. Al-Farra' and others regard them as two forms with the same meaning, and al-Tabari, who prefers the undoubled reading because of the verse's ending, accepts both. The passage closes with a warning to those who deny these signs.

The commentators explain that God reminds people of their origin: He created them from a humble, worthless fluid, the drop of semen, and placed it in a secure and firm place, the womb, until an appointed term known to Him, the time of birth. He then determined their formation, and He is the best of those who determine. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi broadly agree on the meaning: the worthless water is the drop of semen, the firm place is the womb, and the appointed term is the length of pregnancy or the time of birth, which al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud say may be nine months, or less or more.

The reading of the word « faqadarna » is divided. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a doubled letter, meaning « to determine », while the other readers read it without doubling, meaning « to have power ». Al-Tabari considers both readings sound and prefers the single form because the verse ends with « the capable », while noting that the Arabs use both forms. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya lean toward the intensive form, supported by a report attributed to Ibn Mas'ud that explains « the capable » as « the determiners ».

Al-Razi notes that the two forms can mean the same thing and that the phrase can refer either to the greatness of the creation or to its precise measure. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the passage serves as proof that resurrection is possible, since the One who creates with such precision can recreate. The commentators draw no legal ruling from the verse, though Ibn al-Qayyim discusses at length, starting from this water, whether semen is pure or impure.

This passage from Surat al-Mursalat recalls God's power to create. It reminds the disbelievers that He created them from a despised fluid, the seminal drop, and placed it in a secure place, the womb, until a known term set by God, which is the time of birth. The commentators agree on these meanings: the despised water is the semen, the secure place is the womb, and the known term is the time of delivery. The verb 'faqadarna' is read in two ways. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a doubled letter, 'faqaddarna', meaning 'We decreed it with measure, and how excellent are We as decreers.' Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer this reading, supporting it with the verse 'from a drop He created him and measured him'. The other readers have 'faqadarna', meaning 'We had power', a reading that al-Tabari and most readers follow. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba hold that the two forms are synonyms, and al-Tabari notes that the Arabs use both together. Some commentators add other meanings, such as God's measuring of each person's fate, the short or long life, or the happy or unhappy destiny, but these remain secondary views. The passage ends with a warning to those who deny these signs.

This verse announces a dire fate, woe (wayl), for those who deny the truth on the Day of Judgment. It recurs after several passages of the surah and closes a series of proofs of God's power drawn from the creation of man from a lowly fluid, placed in a secure place until an appointed term. The commentators agree that wayl means ruin and severe punishment, and that the deniers are those who reject God's power to resurrect and to requite.

Opinions differ on certain terms. Ibn 'Abbas says the lowly water is the purest essence of water, while Mujahid and Qatada take it as weak water, and Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi understand it as semen. Al-Kalbi and al-Razi identify the secure place as the womb, and Wahb ibn Munabbih stresses that it shields the child from heat and cold. Most read the appointed measure as the time of birth, whereas Ibn Kathir understands it as a term of six or nine months.

Regarding the reading of faqaddarna, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a doubled letter, while Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi consider both readings to share one meaning, and al-Farra' and al-Tabari note that the Arabs use both forms. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi judge the doubled form preferable. Finally, Ibn 'Ashur and Abu al-Su'ud simply note that the woe is tied to God's power.

This verse reminds people of a blessing of God in the form of a rhetorical question: He made the earth a container that gathers the living on its surface, in their homes, and the dead within it, in their graves. The commentators agree that "kifatan" means gathering and containing. Ibn Abbas glosses it as "a covering", Mujahid as "it gathers their refuse and what comes out of them", and al-Sha'bi says: "its belly is for your dead and its back for your living." Al-Tabari holds that the earth holds both the living and the dead, while al-Farra' and Ibn Kathir explain that people are gathered on its surface and in its depths. On the grammar of "living and dead", al-Tabari cites Basran grammarians who take it as a circumstantial accusative, and Kufan grammarians who take it as governed by "kifatan"; he judges the Kufan view more correct. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir report that some followers of al-Shafi'i used the verse to rule that grave-robbers must have their hands cut off, since the grave is a protected place, a view also noted by Ibn Qasim and Ibn Abd al-Barr among the Malikis. As for the firm mountains and sweet water, the commentators see them as signs of God's power, and all of them close with the warning to those who deny.

This verse reminds people of a blessing from God: He made the earth a kifat, meaning a receptacle that gathers the living and the dead. The living dwell on its surface in their homes, and the dead are buried in its depths in graves. Ibn Abbas explains kifat as a shelter or covering, Mujahid as something that covers the body of the dead, and Abu Ubayda and some philologists as a container. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi, agree that the earth gathers both the living and the dead, though they differ on the details. Qatada and al-Sha'bi hold that the living are on its back and the dead in its belly, while Mujahid in one of his views, Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash understand it as a division of the earth itself into living land that produces growth and dead land that does not. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy analyse the grammar: the words ahyaa' and amwatan are objects of kifat or accusatives of circumstance, while al-Farra' explains their case by the effect of the word kifat. Some jurists, including Ibn al-Qasim and Rabi'a, cite the verse to argue that the grave is a protected place, so a grave robber should have his hand cut off, though al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur note that this inference is far-fetched. All agree that the rawasi are firm, lofty mountains and that the furat water is sweet and pleasant to drink.

In this verse God reminds people of His favours on earth by describing the earth as a receptacle that gathers the living on its surface in their homes and the dead within it in their graves. Ibn Abbas understands kifat as a shelter, while Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Qatada say its back is for the living and its belly for the dead; in another view Mujahid takes the living and dead to mean what grows and what does not. Some jurists, as reported by al-Razi and al-Qurtubi from Rabi'a, took the verse to show that the grave is a protected place, so that a grave-robber who steals a shroud deserves the amputation of his hand, and Ibn al-Jawzi notes that Ibn Mas'ud buried a louse in the mosque citing it. The firm mountains are, according to al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, set in the earth so it does not shake, and the commentators describe them as tall and lofty. Sweet water, furat, means pure and pleasant water, and Ibn Abbas and al-Zamakhshari name four great rivers, the Sayhan, the Jayhan, the Nile and the Euphrates. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read the indefinite forms as expressing grandeur and abundance, and Ibn Sa'di notes that these gifts call for gratitude, which is why the verse ends by warning those who deny them.

This verse announces woe, meaning ruin and severe punishment, for those who deny God's blessings on the Day of Judgment. It closes a series of proofs of God's power and generosity. God made the earth a container that gathers the living upon its surface and the dead within it, set firm mountains on it, and gave us sweet water to drink. The commentators see these blessings as calling for gratitude, so denying them is more grave, which explains the threat. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that kifat means gathering and holding, and that the earth shelters the living in their homes and the dead in their graves. Others, such as al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya, also report the reading that the earth brings forth life or dryness. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the indefinite forms express grandeur, while al-Qurtubi notes that some jurists derived from this the rule that a grave-robber should be punished, since the grave is a protected place. On the sweet water, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada define it as pure, sweet water, and Ibn Kathir links it to rain or springs. The commentators generally see the repetition of this verse as emphasis on the punishment, each threat matching a different kind of denial.

On the Day of Resurrection, the deniers will be told, in rebuke and mockery, to go to what they used to deny, namely the punishment of Hell. They will be led to the smoke that rises and then splits into three branches. The commentators agree that this shade offers neither coolness nor protection from the flame, and that Hell hurls sparks of enormous size. Most identify the shade with the smoke of Hell. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada say the three branches surround the deniers from above, from the right and from the left, while al-Dahhak identifies them as the thorny plant, the zaqqum tree and the ghislin, and Ibn Abbas reports that the shade is that of their idol, the three-branched cross. Qatada compares the smoke to an enclosing pavilion. The word "qasr" was understood by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas as a great building or fortress, whereas others, including Ibn Abbas in another report, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak, took it to mean cut logs or the trunks of large palm trees, and one reading gives the sense of palm necks. As for the "yellow camels", al-Tabari, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and most scholars take them to be black camels tinged with yellow, while Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understood ship cables, and Ibn Abbas also reported pieces of copper. The camel meaning is considered the best known in Arabic usage.

On the Day of Judgment, the deniers will be told, in rebuke and mockery: go to what you used to deny, the punishment. They will then be told: go to a shade with three branches. Most commentators, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, take this to be the smoke of Hell, which, as it rises, splits into three parts because of its vastness, and which offers neither shade nor protection from the flame. The verse then describes the Fire hurling sparks as large as a palace, which look like tawny camels. On the general sense of the smoke the commentators agree, but they differ on the three branches: Mujahid says they surround the sinner from above, the right and the left; al-Dahhak identifies them as al-Dari', al-Zaqqum and al-Ghislin; others take them to be the flame, the sparks and the smoke, or the wall of fire that encircles the damned. On the word qasr, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read it as a great building or fortress, others as thick logs stored for winter, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak take it as palm or tree trunks, and some as necks of animals. As for the yellow camels, most, such as al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada, understand black camels tending to yellow, while Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understand ships' cables or pieces of copper. The verse then says that on that day they will not speak to any purpose and will not be permitted to offer excuses, and repeats the woe upon the deniers. Finally they are told that this is the Day of Decision, in which the former and the latter have been gathered, and that if they have any scheme, let them use it.

On the Day of Resurrection the disbelievers are told, in rebuke, to go to the punishment they used to deny. They are led to a shade of three branches, which the commentators explain as the smoke of Hell rising and dividing into three parts because of its immensity. Yet it is no shade that shelters from heat, and it does not shield them from the flame. The scholars describe Hell hurling sparks as large as palaces, resembling yellow camels. They largely agree that the shade is the smoke of Hell and that the negation is said in mockery, since a shade is expected to give relief. They differ on the three branches: Mujahid says they surround the person from above, the right and the left, al-Dahhak says they are the dari', the zaqqum and the ghislin, Qatada identifies them with the canopy of smoke, and others see only a figure for vast size. On the word qasr, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud speak of a great building or fortresses, while others understand thick firewood or palm trunks, and Qatada necks of camels. On the yellow camels, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada take them to be black camels, the view preferred by al-Tabari, whereas Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understand ship cables or pieces of copper. Al-Razi notes that the comparison conveys size, colour and the rapid succession of sparks at once. The verse ends with the woe upon the deniers on the day they will be judged.

On the Day of Resurrection the deniers will be told to go toward what they used to deny, namely the punishment. They will be led to the shade of a smoke from Hell that splits into three branches. This shade offers no coolness and no protection from the flame, and the commentators read this as mocking irony. The verse then describes the sparks Hell throws out as being like a palace in size, and like yellow camels. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Hasan, take the yellow camels to mean black camels with a yellowish tint, and the qasr to mean a great building, while Ibn Abbas, cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Bukhari, explains it as logs of wood that the people of pre-Islamic times cut and stored for winter. Others, such as Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, take the jimalat to be the thick ropes of ships, and Ibn Abbas is also reported to have said they are pieces of copper. Al-Razi argues that the comparison with yellow camels conveys more terror, combining size, number, colour and succession. The readings differ on several words, including jimalat and jumalat and the vowels of qasr. All agree the passage conveys the terror of the punishment.

This verse describes the fire of Hell on the Day of Resurrection, when the deniers are told to go to what they used to deny, namely the punishment. They are directed to the smoke of Hell that splits into three branches, a shade that neither shelters nor protects from the flame. The verse then compares the sparks it throws to a palace in size, and to yellow camels in colour, number, and movement. The commentators agree that the palace comparison conveys magnitude and the camel comparison conveys colour, multitude, and succession. On the word qasr, al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud take it as a lofty building or palaces, Ibn Abbas also reports it as wood stored for winter, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak as the roots of large trees and palms, and Qatada as the necks of camels. On jamalat, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Tabari say black camels, since their blackness tends toward yellow, while Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say ship cables, and a report from Ibn Abbas calls them pieces of copper. The readings differ in the vowel of the jim and in the alif, and each yields a sense. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur cite the verse of Abu al-'Ala al-Ma'arri comparing a spark to a leather tent, and Ibn 'Ashur judges the charge that he meant to rival the Quran to be baseless. The passage closes with woe to the deniers, who can neither offer an excuse nor speak in their defence.

God declares that disaster and severe ruin will fall, on the Day of Judgment, upon those who denied the Resurrection and the recompense. The commentators describe what will be said to them beforehand: they will be told to go toward the punishment they used to deny, to a three-branched shadow of the smoke of Hell, which gives no shade and no protection from the flame. This smoke rises from a fire that hurls sparks as huge as palaces and as yellow as camels in colour and in their successive movement. All agree that the verse is a warning to the deniers and depicts a scene of humiliation. On the meaning of "qasr", the scholars differ: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others take it as a tall building, a fortress or a city, while others, including Qatada and al-Tabari, understand thick firewood or palm trunks. As for the "yellow camels", al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada read them as black camels, Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as ship cables, and a report from Ibn Abbas as chunks of copper; al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi favour black camels. The repeated "woe" has puzzled them: some, such as Abu al-Hasan as cited by al-Tha'alibi, hold that each repetition refers to a different matter, while Ibn Kathir explains that the Day of Judgment has many stages, some of speech and some of silence, and that the deniers will not be permitted to make excuses. The verse ends with a challenge: if they have any scheme, let them carry it out.

This verse announces that on the Day of Judgment the deniers will not speak with any words that could benefit them, and they will not be given permission to offer excuses, because they have none. The commentators explain the phrase "they will not speak" in closely related ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as a denial of speech during some stages of that long day, not throughout it, and they cite other verses where the wrongdoers do speak, such as their plea "Our Lord, bring us out." Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Alusi and al-Biqa'i hold that speech which brings no benefit is as if it were no speech at all. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, relates the verse to a specific moment, such as their entry into the Fire. Al-Razi suggests that the negation should be read in context: they will not produce a valid argument at that time. All agree that the wrongdoers have no excuse and that denial brings punishment, both spiritual and physical. Ibn 'Ashur observes that repeating the warning after each description reinforces its force. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the verb "they would make excuses" is in the nominative because it is coordinated with the preceding clause and is not a consequence of the negation, a point taken up by al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur. The commentators present these different ways of reconciling the verses without deciding between them.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the deniers are not given permission to offer excuses, so no excuse is accepted from them. The commentators agree that they have no valid justification to offer for what they did. Al-Tabari explains that the statement about not speaking applies only to some phases of that long day, not to all of it, and he supports this with the grammar of attaching a day to a verbal clause. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi describe the silence as one state among several that occur on that day. Al-Hasan says they do not speak with any valid argument, even if they do speak. Al-Razi holds that they are not permitted to put forward an excuse that would be false, and that the verb is in the nominative because it is coordinated with the previous clause rather than being its consequence, which avoids the implication that they had a suppressed excuse. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note that the nominative is the reading of most reciters, while the accusative is considered acceptable for the sake of rhyme. Al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the denial of excuse holds regardless of permission. Modern commentators such as Ibn Ashur see the verse as a repetition of the warning found throughout the sura, and Sayyid Qutb views the silence as a sign of dread and humiliation.

This verse announces ruin and severe punishment for the deniers on the Day of Judgment, the Day of Decision when the first and last generations are gathered to be judged. The commentators read this 'woe' as a grave threat to those who deny resurrection, recompense and what the messengers brought. The exegetes agree that the Day has several stations: in some people speak and dispute, in others their mouths are sealed and they do not speak, which is why the Qur'an sometimes mentions their speech and sometimes denies it. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Muqatil explain that the negation does not mean permanent silence, while al-Hasan holds that they do not speak with any convincing proof even if they utter words, and al-Razi understands the negation as the absence of an acceptable excuse. On the word 'fa-ya'taziruna', al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi explain that it is coordinated with 'yu'dhanu' and is not an answer to the negation, the rhythm of the verse-endings guiding that choice; al-Farra' holds that the nominative and the subjunctive are both permissible. The refrain 'Woe on that day to the deniers' returns after each scene of the surah; al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari see a fresh meaning in each repetition, a threat and a rebuke. It is repeated because each scene describes a different aspect of the Day of Judgment.

This verse tells those who denied the Resurrection that the Day of Judgment is the Day of Decision, the day when God separates creatures and distinguishes the righteous from the wrongdoers. The commentators agree that "We have gathered you" addresses the disbelievers of this community, and "the former ones" refers to the peoples who denied their prophets before them. Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and others say that the gathering includes both the contemporaries of the Prophet and the earlier nations. Ibn Kathir stresses that the Qur'an here brings together all the condemned for judgment.

As for "If you have any scheme, then scheme against Me", most commentators read it as a rebuke and a challenge: if you have any way of escape, try it. Ibn 'Abbas and others understand it as a call to fight, while Muqatil reads it as a simple invitation to seek a way out. Al-Qurtubi reports that some attribute the phrase to the Prophet, as Hud said to his people. Al-Razi sees it as a spiritual punishment, since they can no longer use the deceptions they relied on in the world.

The scholars therefore agree that the plain meaning is an announcement of judgment and a humiliation of the deniers, who have no escape left. Their differences concern mainly who is meant by "We have gathered you" and how the scheme mentioned should be understood.

God addresses the deniers on the Day of Resurrection, after describing to them the torment of the Fire: this is the Day of Judgment, when God separates creatures and distinguishes truth from falsehood. We have gathered you and all who came before you among the deniers; if you have any scheme to escape punishment, then use it. The commentators agree that the verse is a rebuke and a challenge to their helplessness. Al-Tabari understands the kayd as a stratagem for escaping punishment, while al-Zamakhshari sees it as a public confirmation of their weakness after their plotting against God's religion and its people. Ibn Abbas and Muqatil keep the sense of saving oneself. Al-Qurtubi reports that Ibn Abbas read it as an invitation to fight, and that some attribute the words to the Prophet, in the manner of Hud's challenge. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di read it as a severe threat: no one can escape God's grasp, as the verse on jinn and humans affirms. Ibn Kathir also cites a report from Ubada ibn al-Samit about the gathering on one plain. Al-Razi holds that this rebuke is a spiritual punishment, harder on the intellect than bodily suffering, and Ibn Ashur sees it as a reminder of their past misconduct. The passage closes with the refrain repeated: woe that day to the deniers.

This verse declares that ruin and severe punishment await those who deny the Day of Resurrection, judgment and recompense. The commentators explain that the word wayl means destruction and misery that result from denial. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that this warning applies to anyone who denies what God has reported about these people and their fate. The verse recurs after each scene of the Hereafter described in the surah, and the commentators see it as a refrain of threat and rebuke.

The exegetes agree that this passage is a sequence of reproaches. They are told to proceed to a shade with three branches, on a day when they will not speak and no excuse will be granted, and then to a Day of Decision when earlier and later generations are gathered together. Al-Razi explains that this is the day when every judgment is delivered, both between the servant and his Lord and between people themselves. He reads the phrase "if you have any scheme, then use it" as a humiliating rebuke, since they know that no trick will help them then. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan share this reading of censure and of their exposed helplessness.

Ibn 'Ashur holds that the repetition of the verset reinforces the threat and connects to what precedes it, and Ibn Sa'di notes that the torment of the soul is more painful than physical suffering. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the repetition is not mere redundancy, since each occurrence addresses a different content.

This verse describes the reward of the God-fearing, who perform their duties and avoid what is forbidden: they will be in shade and beside flowing springs, with fruits of their desire, and it will be said to them, eat and drink with pleasure for what you used to do. The commentators agree on the general meaning of a complete happiness free from harm. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the shades as the shade of trees and dwellings, which protect from heat and cold, while Ibn 'Atiyya explains that shade in Paradise refers to the density of trees and the quality of the buildings, since no sun harms there. Al-Sam'ani holds that the air of Paradise, free of any discomfort, serves as shade even without a sun. Al-Razi argues that the God-fearing are those who guard against polytheism, a view he supports by the coherence of the surah, and al-Qurtubi follows this reading. Al-Tabari adds that the word wholesome means that the food and drink are lasting and bring no harm. The point of the verse is that the reward matches good deeds and is given as an honour to believers. Several scholars, including Ibn 'Atiyya, also connect this passage with the contrast to the shade of smoke reserved for the disbelievers.

This verse describes what the righteous will receive in the Hereafter: shade under dense trees, flowing springs, and fruits they desire. Most commentators understand the righteous as those who avoided polytheism, performed their duties and abstained from what is forbidden, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim explain. The phrase "that which they desire" means that they obtain whatever they wish, without fear of harm or bad consequences, unlike worldly food, which people eat only as it is available, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim. Most take "fawakih" to mean all kinds of fruit, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that the particle "min" indicates these fruits are added to other desired pleasures. On the command to eat and drink, al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari take it as something said to them, al-Razi sees it as an honouring favour rather than an obligation, and Ibn 'Ashur compares it to a host welcoming guests. Al-Baghawi and al-Razi explain that "hanii'an" means pure enjoyment, free of disturbance. The commentators agree that this picture is set against the fate of the deniers, announced by the refrain "woe that day to those who deny."

This verse, within the description of the bliss of the God-fearing, says that they will be told in the Hereafter to eat and drink with pleasure, as a reward for what they did in this world. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that this food and drink is lasting and causes no harm, and that this honour is given as a kindness to them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the phrase « eat and drink » as a circumstantial clause describing the pious, meaning that they are told this. Al-Razi reads the particle « bima » as indicating cause: their good deeds are the reason for this good. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani agree, and Ibn 'Ashur sees the words as addressed either to the pious, or to the disbelievers as a way of grieving them. On who the « pious » are, al-Razi reports that Muqatil and al-Kalbi understand them as those who guard against associating partners with God, and he favours this view; al-Tabari widens the meaning to performing the obligations and avoiding the forbidden. Several commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, connect what follows to the unbelievers of Mecca. No legal ruling is drawn from this passage. The commentators stress above all that the reward matches the goodness of one's conduct, and the warning of woe for those who deny it.

This verse describes the reward of the righteous and the good-doers in the next life, following the account of the punishment of the deniers. The commentators explain that the God-fearing, those who guarded against God's punishment by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions, will be in shade, beside springs and fruits of their desire, and it will be said to them: eat and drink with delight for what you did. The phrase 'Thus do We reward the good-doers' means that just as the God-fearing receive this bounty, those who do good in their obedience and worship will receive it too.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take the God-fearing to be those who fulfilled the duties and avoided the prohibitions. Muqatil and al-Kalbi understand them as those who guarded against associating partners with God, and al-Razi adopts this reading, arguing that the whole surah rebukes the disbelievers and so the promise to the believers must match that theme. Al-Hasan al-Basri defines the good-doers as those who performed all the obligations and avoided all the prohibitions. Al-Qurtubi says they are those who believed well in the Prophet and acted well.

The commentators agree that the shade of Paradise is not meant to protect from the heat of the sun. Ibn 'Atiyya explains it as the density of the trees and the excellence of the dwellings. They differ on the force of 'eat and drink'. Abu Hashim takes it as a real command, while Abu 'Ali takes it as an honour and not a legal obligation. Al-Razi notes that the particle 'bi' in 'for what you used to do' marks a sign or cause rather than a right earned. Ibn 'Ashur sees the phrase 'hanii'an' as a blessing of welcome meaning pure pleasure without disturbance.

This verse sets the fate of the God-conscious against that of the deniers. The commentators explain that the pious will be in shade, beside springs and fruits they desire, and it will be said to them: eat and drink with pleasure for what you did; this is how God rewards the good-doers. The phrase that follows, woe on that day to the deniers, is read by Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di as a threat to those who rejected this promise and this honour given to the pious; al-Sa'di adds that the deprivation of this bliss alone would be enough to grieve them. On the meaning of 'the God-conscious', al-Tabari and al-Sam'ani take it as those who perform the obligations and avoid the prohibitions, whereas al-Razi, following the context of the whole surah which rebukes the unbelievers, restricts it to those who avoided polytheism. Al-Tabari understands the shade as protection from heat and cold, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari describe it as the density of trees and buildings in paradise, with no scorching sun. Al-A'raj's reading 'zulal' is noted. Al-Tabari explains 'hanî'' as free from disturbance or harm. On the repetition of the refrain, al-Razi and al-Tha'alibi note that each occurrence targets a different subject, making it a renewed warning. The commentators agree the verse functions as a threat through reproach and humiliation, though the occasions of revelation for passages about prayer, attributed by some to Thaqif or to the hypocrites, remain debated.

In this verse God addresses those who deny the Resurrection with a tone of threat and warning: eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while, for you are criminals, and your end will be the punishment that befell the criminals of earlier nations. The commentators agree that the imperative here carries the sense of warning rather than permission, and that the word 'little' describes worldly enjoyment however long it lasts. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Zayd, take the address to be to the disbelievers, and Ibn Juzayy likewise addresses it to the unbelievers, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya relate that it concerns the Quraysh of Mecca. On the words 'And when it is said to them: bow down, they do not bow,' the scholars differ. Ibn 'Abbas, as cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, holds that this will be said on the Day of Resurrection when they are called to prostrate and cannot. Mujahid and Qatada place it in this life and understand bowing as prayer, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as humility and submission to God; al-Zamakhshari notes that the Arabs disliked bowing and prostration. Muqatil ties the verse to the Thaqif tribe, who refused to pray. As for 'Then in what discourse after this will they believe?', most commentators explain that whoever does not believe in the inimitable Qur'an will not believe in any other book. The refrain 'Woe that day to the deniers' recurs, and al-Razi explains that each occurrence is meant to convey a different sense.

This verse declares that ruin, a severe punishment, awaits those who denied the truth on the Day of Judgment. Most commentators read it as a refrain repeated throughout the surah after each description of the Hereafter, and they agree that the addressees are those who rejected the resurrection, the messengers and the Quran. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that scholars asked why it recurs, and answer that each occurrence is meant to convey a different sense, as Abu Hayyan and others also record.

The commentators differ on the context. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the preceding verse as a threat to the disbelievers: they will enjoy this world briefly and then go to the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that the phrase may describe a state in which the punishment is already fixed at the moment they are told to eat and enjoy. Ibn 'Atiyya links the verses to the Quraysh of Mecca, while he mentions that some assign them to the hypocrites of Medina.

The verse about bowing also receives several readings. Mujahid and al-Tabari take it as a command to pray, while Ibn Abbas and others place it on the Day of Judgment when they will be called to prostrate and will be unable to. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya report that it refers to the tribe of Thaqif, who refused to bow, and they note that bowing can stand for the whole prayer. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya draw from the verse that unbelievers are bound by the obligations of the law.

This verse describes people who, when told to bow down, refuse to do so. Most commentators take bowing (rukū') to mean prayer, since bowing is one of its essential parts. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and the Tafsir al-Jalalayn follow this reading, and Ibn Kathir explains it as refusing to pray with the congregation. Others, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Qasimi, read it more broadly as humbling oneself before God, accepting His revelation and abandoning arrogance.

The main disagreement concerns the timing. Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, says it refers to the Day of Resurrection, when the disbelievers are called to prostrate and cannot, because they never prostrated to God in the world. Qatada places it in this world and urges believers to perform the bowing well. Ibn Juzayy considers the worldly reading more apparent while noting the other view. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that these words may be addressed in the Hereafter as a reminder of what they neglected in life.

Some commentators link the verse to a specific occasion. Al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi report that it was revealed about the tribe of Thaqif, who refused prayer and said that bowing would be a disgrace to them. The Prophet replied that there is no good in a religion without bowing and prostration. Al-Qurtubi also cites Ibn al-Arabi, who takes the verse as evidence that bowing is a pillar of prayer.

Al-Razi draws from the verse that commands are obligatory and that disbelievers are bound by the branches of the law, a point Ibn 'Ashur rejects because the meaning of 'those who pray' is not fixed here. The verse ends with a warning of woe for those who deny, and asks in what message they could believe after the Qur'an.

This verse repeats a warning of ruin and punishment for those who deny the messengers and what they announce. Several commentators note that the refrain returns after each statement in the surah, so that every announcement is accompanied by the threat. Al-Razi and al-Biqa'i hold that the repetition is not idle: each return concerns a different matter, or it serves to emphasize the warning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir specify that these are people who reject God's announcement of resurrection and judgment. Opinions differ on the time intended. Ibn 'Abbas and others understand the call to bow down on the Day of Resurrection, which the disbelievers cannot answer, as the occasion, while Qatada and Mujahid place it in this world. The meaning of ruku' is also debated: most take it to mean prayer, while some read it as humility before the truth. Many commentators, including Ibn Kathir, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Qasimi, conclude from the last phrase that the Qur'an is the greatest of accounts, so whoever rejects it will find no other discourse to believe in.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the surah as a rebuke: if these people do not believe in the Quran, which is clear in its proof and unmatched in its eloquence, then in what discourse will they believe after it? In other words, whoever rejects the most manifest speech cannot be expected to accept any other. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the reference to be the Quran itself, while al-Razi stresses that the word hadith designates these very words, whose inimitability is the basis of their authority.

The exegetes agree that the verse belongs to a context of threat and reproach. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani note that the pronoun in "after it" refers to the Quran, and that the verse combines censure with astonishment at those who turn away from it. Al-Baghawi and Abu Hayyan take the passage to concern the Quraysh, whereas others link the preceding verses to the hypocrites or to the tribe of Thaqif.

Readers differ on the verb. Most read "yu'minun" in the third person, while Ya'qub and, according to some, Ibn 'Amir read "tu'minun" in the second person, as Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi report. Ibn Kathir and al-Shinqiti cite a hadith transmitted through Abu Hurayra that whoever recites this passage should say: I believe in God and in what He has sent down. The commentators do not rule on the strength of this report.

As for the repetition of "Woe that day to the deniers", al-Samani, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di see it as emphasis meant to warn, while others hold that each repetition carries a different meaning.
